opus-5.5.text:
Looking back, I think that experience shaped me much more than I realized at the time. When you start something as an undergraduate, you don't really know what you don't know. That's both the biggest weakness and, honestly, the biggest advantage. You're not afraid, because you haven't failed enough times yet to be afraid.

What I learned most wasn't really technical. In school, problems are well-defined: someone gives you the question, and there's a correct answer. In a company, nobody tells you what the question is. You have to figure out what problem is actually worth solving, whether anyone cares about it, and whether you're the right person to solve it. That shift in thinking, from solving given problems to finding the right problems, has stayed with me ever since, including in research.

There was also a lot of humility involved. Things you think will take a week take three months. People you thought would be excited aren't. You learn very quickly that a good idea is maybe ten percent of the work, and the rest is execution, persistence, and a little bit of luck.

If I'm honest, I don't think I would call it a big success in the commercial sense. But I don't regret it at all. It taught me how to work with people, how to make decisions without complete information, and how to keep going when things aren't working. Later, when I moved into research, especially robotics, where so much fails before something works, that resilience turned out to be really valuable.

So my view is: if a young person has the chance and the curiosity, it's worth trying. The cost of failing at twenty is quite low, and what you learn is something you can't really get from a classroom.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when I look back on it now, I think the most valuable thing wasn't the company itself, it was how early it forced me to face reality.

When you're an undergraduate, you have this feeling that you can do anything. You've been good at exams your whole life, and you assume the world works the same way: you work hard, you get the result. Starting a company is the first time that assumption gets completely broken. You work extremely hard and nothing happens. Or you do something casually and it takes off. There's no teacher, no syllabus, and no one is going to grade you fairly. That was a shock for me, but a very useful one.

The second thing is that I had almost no idea what I didn't know. I thought the hard part was the technology. I spent most of my time writing code and almost no time thinking about who would actually pay for it, how we would reach them, or whether the problem I was solving was a real problem or just one that I personally found interesting. We ended up building something that was technically fine and commercially almost irrelevant. That lesson stayed with me much longer than any lesson about engineering.

And then there's the people side. At that age you start a company with your friends because they're the people around you. That's wonderful for about six months. Then you discover that being good friends and being good co-founders are completely different things. You have to learn how to disagree, how to divide responsibility, how to have a conversation where someone's feelings are going to get hurt and the company still needs to move forward the next morning. I did that badly at first. I think most people do.

So would I say it was a success? Not in the conventional sense. We didn't build something large, and eventually I moved on. But if you ask whether it was worth it, absolutely. The cost of failing at twenty is extremely low. You have no mortgage, no family depending on you, and your peers are mostly still in class. Everything you lose is recoverable. Everything you learn, you keep.

The one thing I'd caution against is doing it because it's fashionable. I saw a lot of people around me start companies because that was what ambitious people were supposed to do, not because there was something they couldn't stop thinking about. Those companies tended to disappear quietly. If you're going to do it, you should do it because the problem bothers you enough that you'd be working on it anyway.

astra-6.text:
Looking back, I see it as an education in taking responsibility. As an undergraduate, you’re used to having a clearly defined problem and being judged on your answer. Starting a company means you have to figure out which problem is worth solving in the first place—and whether anyone actually needs what you’re building.

Being young gives you the willingness to try, but it also means there’s a lot you don’t know. For me, the value of that experience was learning to test my assumptions, listen to other people, and adjust. I wouldn’t say every undergraduate should start a company, but it can be a valuable way to discover both what you want to do and what you still need to learn.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes starting a company as an education and a way to learn, but does not say Jie Tan chose to do it to discover firsthand what entrepreneurship was like.

sol-6.1.text:
Looking back, I see it as a valuable learning experience. As an undergraduate, you’re used to problems with fairly clear boundaries. Starting a company means figuring out which problems matter, whether anyone needs what you’re building, and how to work with other people to make it happen. You have to learn while making decisions with incomplete information.

Being young gives you the courage to try, but enthusiasm alone isn’t enough. For me, the value of that experience is learning to listen, take responsibility, and adjust when an idea doesn’t work.
